display: I run Casa Prato, a small tableware shop in Alfama, Lisbon. I sketch my own plates and bowls and I'm looking for makers who can produce them in small batches.

signals.text: I need a ceramic maker in Portugal who can produce small batches, around 50 pieces per glaze, of stoneware I've designed.
I have six winter tableware designs fully sketched (soup bowls, low plates, a lidded pot, two cup sizes) and nobody to make them.
I want glazes that look like wet stone and celadon, with the kiln marks left visible, and I'm looking for a potter or workshop who can do that.
Customers keep asking for pieces that look hand-thrown, with a thumbprint or a flame mark. Three people asked in one week, and one would pay double.
The Aveiro workshop that made my stoneware for four years closed in August. I have a spreadsheet of nine replacements and four are crossed out.
The one factory that answered wants a 500-piece minimum per glaze. I sell about 60 of each design per season, so the numbers don't work.
I'd like the winter collection in the shop by early December, but that's looking unlikely.
A Chiado restaurant wants my grey-green bowls and deep bowls again and is willing to wait until spring.
I keep ordering perfect, factory-made things when what people want to buy is something with a visible hand in it.
I'd like a tutor or language partner for Portuguese who actually shows up. My intermediate level holds me back with suppliers.
I'm training for a 10k along the Tagus on October 11 and would like a running partner. My knee clicks.
The missed autumn restocks have cost me about 4,000 euros so far, and the shop's margin is thin.
My landlord wants to turn the flat upstairs into a short-term rental and has hinted the shop's ceiling needs structural work. I'm waiting for his letter and I'm worried about it.
I'm tired. Shop, supplier and lease all landed together, and people close to me are suggesting I give up and go back to interior design.

offers.text: A finished, drawn design brief for each piece: dimensions, profile, glaze colour cards and references. I sketch every piece before ordering it.
A sketchbook archive of about 400 plate and bowl designs, which could become a shared line with a maker.
Eleven years of experience designing restaurant interiors and specifying tableware in Rotterdam and Amsterdam. I can advise cafés and restaurants on tableware and spaces.
A retail outlet for makers: a 38 m² shop with a blue door in Alfama and an online shop shipping across the EU.
A newsletter of 2,700 subscribers with a 41% open rate, where I can tell the story of a maker and their pieces.
Reorder relationships with eight restaurants in Lisbon and Porto that buy tableware every season. I could introduce a reliable maker to them.
Reliable, repeat small orders. I can commit to a steady pace of around 50 to 60 pieces per design per season for a maker who fits.
I can collaborate in Dutch, English, Portuguese (intermediate) or some German, and host visitors in the shop.

catchers.hypo: Hi, I'm a potter near Coimbra. I throw stoneware in celadon and ash glazes and I've never had a retailer who wanted 50 pieces rather than 500. Is that of interest?
catchers.can: Anouk can send the six winter sketches and colour cards, discuss a small trial run of the celadon flat-rim bowl, and promote the maker in her shop and newsletter.
catchers.confirm: Can you produce a run of roughly 50 pieces per glaze, thrown or hand-finished, in Portugal, and do you accept designs drawn by someone else?

catchers.hypo: I run a small ceramics studio and we have kiln space and a spare slot this season. We'd like to make something designed by somebody else.
catchers.can: Anouk can offer a ready design brief for a short production run and a retail channel with a story attached.
catchers.confirm: Would you accept a first order below 100 pieces per design, with delivery before the first week of December?

catchers.hypo: I was an apprentice at a workshop in Aveiro and am now looking for a place to keep making stoneware. Do you know anyone who needs a maker?
catchers.can: Anouk can get in touch through Sr. Matos, the retired Aveiro workshop owner, who knows the local ceramics community, and can put the person in front of her small-batch needs.
catchers.confirm: Are you or the people you'd introduce experienced in stoneware production around Aveiro, and willing to work to small quantities?

catchers.hypo: I own a café in Lisbon and want matching plates and cups with character, not catalogue stuff. Can you help?
catchers.can: Anouk can specify and supply tableware drawn for the space, and through her friend Ana, who runs a bakery, can reach other small food businesses that buy by the season.
catchers.confirm: Is your order a few dozen pieces per item, for a food business in Portugal, with some flexibility on lead time?

catchers.hypo: I'm a restaurant owner opening a new place in Porto and want tableware that looks handmade, in small enough quantities to fit a young kitchen.
catchers.can: Anouk can design and source a custom set and use her existing restaurant relationships as a reference.
catchers.confirm: Do you need a custom or semi-custom tableware set for a restaurant in Portugal at fewer than about 100 pieces per item?

catchers.hypo: I run a studio in Utrecht and know several ceramic makers in the Netherlands who would like a Lisbon outlet or a collaboration abroad.
catchers.can: Anouk is Dutch and can compare pieces with her sketches and consider stocking a few pieces or a shared line, though she prefers a maker whose work she can see being made.
catchers.confirm: Is the work handmade or hand-finished, and can the maker ship small quantities to Portugal?

catchers.hypo: I'm a short-term-rental host in Lisbon who wants a tasteful, locally made tableware set for guests, not something from a big box store.
catchers.can: Anouk can put together a set from her shop and ship it, using the pieces she already stocks.
catchers.confirm: Are you after a complete tableware set for a rental flat in Portugal, rather than a single decorative piece?

catchers.hypo: I'm a designer who also runs a small shop and would like to hear how you manage a collection when your maker disappears and minimums are too high.
catchers.can: Anouk can share what she has learned about small-batch minimums and how to compare makers, and share her supplier spreadsheet logic.
catchers.confirm: Are you facing a supplier-minimum or supplier-loss problem as an independent shop, rather than a product-design question?

forbids.text: I won't stock anything mass-produced in Asia, even though that rule is currently costing me.
I can't commit to minimums of 500 pieces per glaze or per design; my volume doesn't support it.
I can't hold more than about 6,000 euros of inventory at one time.
I'm closed on Mondays and don't take meetings that day.
I need winter pieces in by early December to sell them in season.
I'm not looking to give up the shop and go back to interior design.

projects.name: Winter collection 2026
projects.text: Six hand-finished tableware designs for the cold months, with wet-stone and celadon glazes and visible kiln marks. They are sketched and need a maker for small runs.

projects.name: Supplier replacement
projects.text: Replace the closed Aveiro stoneware workshop with one or two makers who accept orders of around 50 pieces per glaze.
roles_needed: potter or small workshop in Portugal
intro from the Aveiro ceramics community
shared-minimum partner (another shop that could pool orders)

policy.t1: When there is a real lead, I'll share order volumes, minimum quantities, timelines, my design sketches and the details of the supplier situation.
policy.t2: Once trust is established and I know who I'm dealing with, I'll share the shop's financial situation, the lease worry and how this is affecting me personally.
policy.never: Family money matters, bank details, and anything about my family's finances or debts.
